Here are the verse-by-verse notes, compiled from the sources I was able to access:

---

## 1 Samuel 6 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### v. 1: "When the ark of the LORD had been in the land of the Philistines seven months…"

- **The seven-month duration** shows how reluctant the Philistines were to part with their "trophy." They kept the ark despite the plagues, perhaps hoping their god Dagon would eventually prevail. It can take a long time for people to realize the futility of resisting God. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-6/)
- **Ellicott** notes that during these seven months the ark was moved from temple to temple among the Philistine cities, but the same doom followed it. The LXX (Septuagint) adds here, "and the land swarmed with mice." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/6.htm)
- **Bergen** (cited by Precept Austin) suggests the number seven may carry symbolic overtones of "completeness" or "the perfect work of God," indicating that "when the time of exile allotted by God had been fulfilled…" the ark returned. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-6-commentary)
- **Keil & Delitzsch** observe that the ark had "brought destruction to all the towns to which it had been taken" during these seven months, and that the Hebrew phrase "in the country" is literally "in the fields" of the Philistines. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/1-samuel-6.html)

---

### v. 2: "…the Philistines summoned the priests and diviners, saying, 'What shall we do with the ark of the LORD? Tell us how to send it back to its place.'"

- The Philistines called upon two groups — **priests** and **diviners**. Diviners (Hebrew *qasam*) were a class of religious leaders who practiced occult methods to predict the future or discern hidden knowledge. Israelites were forbidden to consult them (Deut 18:10, 14). (https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-6-commentary)
- **Ellicott** explains that diviners "plied their strange trade, now with the aid of arrows, now with the entrails of slain animals, now with observation of the stars." He notes the irony that the English version translates the same Hebrew word as "prudent" in Isaiah 3:2, "possibly owing to the translators being displeased at finding the professors of a forbidden art ranked so highly among the chosen people." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/6.htm)
- The Philistine rulers understood that sending away an offended and powerful deity was not to be undertaken lightly; doing it improperly might provoke Yahweh even more. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-6-commentary)
- This section contains the **longest recorded dialogue by Philistines in the Bible** (120 words in Hebrew). (https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-6-commentary)

---

### v. 3: "They replied, 'If you return the ark of the God of Israel, do not send it away empty, but by all means return it to Him with a guilt offering…'"

- The priests advised **propitiating Yahweh with gifts**, imagining He was offended at being placed in an inferior position in Dagon's temple. They thought of Him as a "childish, capricious deity" like their own gods. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/6.htm)
- **Keil & Delitzsch** note that the Hebrew term *asham* (guilt offering) is used as a "compensation and satisfaction to be rendered to the God of Israel for the robbery committed upon Him by the removal of the ark." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/1-samuel-6.html)
- **Bergen** (Precept Austin) points out an irony: the Philistine diviners demonstrated knowledge of Torah concepts like guilt offerings, yet their recommended means were "totally wrongheaded" — they missed the requirement of a slain ram (Lev 5:15) and instead recommended golden images, violating the Decalogue's prohibition against likenesses (Exod 20:4). Their advice "represents a syncretistic blend of pagan imitative magic and perverted Torah ritual." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-6-commentary)
- The conditional "then you will be healed" (Keil reads it as conditional) reflects the priests' uncertainty — they did not know for certain that Yahweh was the cause of the plagues. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/1-samuel-6.html)

---

### v. 4–5: "Five gold tumors and five gold rats… according to the number of rulers of the Philistines…"

- It was a **common ancient custom** to offer to the deity likenesses of the diseased body parts. Shipwreck survivors offered pictures to Neptune; gladiators offered weapons to Hercules; even Christians in the 4th–5th centuries (Theodoret records) would offer gold or silver hands, feet, or eyes in churches as thank-offerings for cures. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/6.htm); (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/1-samuel-6.html)
- **Ellicott** notes that v. 5 is the **first mention of the plague of mice in the Hebrew text** (the LXX had previously added the detail). Aristotle and Pliny both mention vast mouse devastations in warm Mediterranean countries. In Egypt, the mouse was the hieroglyphic for destruction. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/6.htm)
- **Keil & Delitzsch** explain that the presentation of images of the things with which they had been chastised was "a kind of fine or compensation for the fault that had been committed against the Deity, to mitigate His wrath." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/1-samuel-6.html)
- **David Guzik** observes that the Philistines gave glory to God by acknowledging His judgment — yet they did not worship Him instead of their own gods. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-6/)
- **Ligonier** (Reformed) notes the Philistine priests were employing "sympathetic magic" — by sending the tumors and rats away, they thought they would send the plague out of their land. (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/ark-returns-to-israel)

---

### v. 6: "Why harden your hearts as the Egyptians and Pharaoh hardened theirs?…"

- The Philistine priests cited the **Exodus tradition**, showing that the account of Israel's deliverance from Egypt had made a deep impression on surrounding nations. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/6.htm)
- **Keil & Delitzsch** note there is "nothing strange" in this reference from pagan priests: the report of those occurrences had spread among all neighboring nations (see 1 Sam 4:8). Even the possibility that Yahweh was behind the plagues was enough to make it advisable to do everything to mitigate His wrath. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/1-samuel-6.html)
- **Guzik**: "Even in a purely self-interested sense, it isn't smart to harden your heart against the LORD." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-6/)

---

### v. 7–9: "Now, therefore, prepare one new cart with two milk cows that have never been yoked…"

- **A new cart** was used in reverence to the ark — a right and true feeling. So also our Lord rode on a colt "whereon never man sat" and was laid in a new tomb (Mark 11:2; Matt 27:60). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/6.htm)
- **Keil & Delitzsch**: The new cart and unyoked animals "corresponded to the holiness of the ark of God." Using an old cart or yoked animals "would have been an offence against the holy thing." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/1-samuel-6.html)
- **The test was stacked against God**: (1) cows never yoked should resist the yoke; (2) milk cows separated from their calves should, by maternal instinct, return home rather than walk toward Israel. The Philistines "forced" God to do something miraculous if He were truly behind the plagues. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-6/)
- **Guzik** notes that though God never wanted the ark transported by cart (He commanded it be carried by poles — Num 4:14-15), "God winked at it in them, both because they were ignorant of God's law to the contrary, and because they had no Levites to carry it upon their shoulders" (citing Poole). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-6/)
- **Ellicott**: The diviners expected the cows would return to their stalls. If instead they went toward Israel, "this would be a sign that they were driven and guided by a Divine power." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/6.htm)
- On **chance**: Guzik argues at length that "chance has no power." He cites the example of a coin flip: chance is just a probability, not a causal force. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-6/)

---

### v. 10–12: "And the cows headed straight up the road toward Beth-shemesh… lowing as they went…"

- **A remarkable miracle**: Two untrained cows, separated from their calves, with no driver, walked ~10 miles on a road they had never traveled, never turning aside to feed or go back to their young. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-6/)
- **"Lowing as they went"** (*ga-ah* in Hebrew): The Theological Wordbook of the OT notes this root "indicates an intense aversion which is expressed often in punitive or adverse action." The cows were grieving for their calves, yet they obeyed God's leading. Guzik: "Even in obedience, we can experience internal conflict, yet we serve a God with good purpose." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-6/)
- **Ellicott**: "The dumb beasts did what the idol priests and diviners scarcely considered possible, for God's hand drove them. The narrative here throughout is evidently unadorned, very easy and natural… telling its story of the Divine interference of the 'Glorious Arm' with exquisite simplicity and truth." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/6.htm)
- **Keil & Delitzsch** observe that the Philistine priests "unconsciously and against their will furnished the occasion for the living God to display His divine glory before those who did not know Him." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/1-samuel-6.html)
- **The Pulpit Commentary** (Homiletics): "God's favour often comes by the most unlikely agencies and means. His power is universal, and all things serve him." It also notes the contrast: "Two kine knew their owner as Hophni and Phinehas knew him not" (Lightfoot). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/1_samuel/6.htm)

---

### v. 13–14: "Now the people of Beth-shemesh were harvesting wheat in the valley… they were overjoyed at the sight."

- **Beth-shemesh** ("House of the Sun") was a **priestly city** (Joshua 21:16), so priests and Levites were on hand — fitting for receiving the ark. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/6.htm)
- **The wheat harvest** places this event in **May–June**. The people were engaged in ordinary secular work, not thinking of the ark, when suddenly they saw it approaching. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/1_samuel/6.htm)
- **Guzik** compares their joy to that of the disciples encountering the risen Jesus — they felt God had "returned from the dead," though He had never truly left them. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-6/)
- **The great stone** in Joshua's field: most likely a natural rock rising from the soil; its presence caused the cart to stop there. This stone became a memorial. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/6.htm)
- **They chopped up the cart and offered the cows as a burnt offering.** Guzik notes this was expensive — cows and carts were valuable property — but they knew it was right to honor God. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-6/)
- **Strictly speaking, the offering violated Mosaic law**: (1) female animals were offered, which was forbidden for burnt offerings (Lev 1:3; 22:19); (2) the sacrifice was made away from the tabernacle (Deut 12:5-6). Yet God honored their hearts and the remarkable circumstances. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-6/)
- **Keil & Delitzsch**, however, argue the sacrifice at Beth-shemesh was **not a violation** because the ark of the covenant itself was present — "the throne of the gracious presence of God, before which the sacrifices were really offered at the tabernacle." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/1-samuel-6.html)
- **Ellicott** agrees: "the offering of these sacrifices at Beth-shemesh, although the Tabernacle never had been stationed there, was no transgression against the law, for now the Ark of the Covenant was present, the occasional throne of the glory-presence of the Eternal, before which the sacrifices were really offered." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/6.htm)

---

### v. 15: "And the Levites took down the ark of the LORD and the chest containing the gold objects…"

- The Israelites were **careful to let the Levites handle the ark**, as commanded (Num 4:1-6, 15). Beth-shemesh being a priestly city meant Levites were available. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-6/)
- **Keil & Delitzsch** render v. 15 as a pluperfect: the Levites had already taken down the ark while the people were sacrificing the cart and cows. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/1-samuel-6.html)

---

### v. 16–18: The guilt offering inventory; the five rulers return to Ekron.

- **The five Philistine rulers** (lords) witnessed the reception of the ark from a distance and then returned to Ekron the same day. Their mission was accomplished, and the question about the source of the plagues was solved. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/6.htm)
- **The golden tumors**: one for each of the five principal cities — Ashdod, Gaza, Ashkelon, Gath, and Ekron. Although only three cities are mentioned as hosting the ark in ch. 5, it likely visited all five during the seven months. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/6.htm)
- **The golden rats** were far more numerous than the five the priests originally recommended (v. 4). Keil explains that "the Philistines offered as many images of mice as there were towns and villages in their five states, no doubt because the plague of mice had spread over the whole land, whereas the plague of boils had only fallen upon the inhabitants of those towns to which the ark of the covenant had come." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/1-samuel-6.html)
- **"The large rock… stands to this day"**: A textual issue. The Hebrew text here is "hopelessly corrupt" per Ellicott. The LXX reads "and this great stone… is a witness unto this day." If the Hebrew *Abel* ("mourning") is original, Kimchi conjectured the stone was called "the great mourning" because of the calamity in v. 19. Keil prefers emending *Abel* to *eben* (stone) and *v'ad* to *v'ed* (witness): "And the great stone is witness to this day." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/6.htm); (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/1-samuel-6.html)

---

### v. 19: "But God struck down some of the people of Beth-shemesh because they looked inside the ark of the LORD…"

This verse is the most contested in the chapter, both textually and interpretively.

#### What was the sin?
- **Guzik** says they "looked into" the ark — opened it and peered inside. Only Kohathite Levites could handle the ark (Num 4:15), and even they could not look inside. The Philistines showed more reverence than the Israelites, who had God's law and should have known better. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-6/)
- **Keil & Delitzsch** disagree, arguing that "looked at" (*ra'ah* with *b*) means "a foolish staring, which was incompatible with the holiness of the ark of God," not actually opening it — "if this had been the meaning, the opening would certainly not have been passed over without notice" in the text. They connect the punishment to the warning of Num 4:20. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/1-samuel-6.html)
- **Ellicott** favors the "looked into" reading (the "favourite Rabbinical explanation") and suggests the chief men, "heated with wine" after the festive sacrifices, "lost all sense of reverence, and determined to use this opportunity of gazing into that sacred chest of which they had heard so much." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/6.htm)
- **Ligonier** (Reformed): "They treated the ark with contempt, handling it even though only the Kohathites… were supposed to touch it. That they did so should not surprise us, for the Israelites had lost the ark in the first place by treating it as a magical talisman." (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/ark-returns-to-israel)

#### The number: 70 or 50,070?
- The BSB text reads "seventy men" with a footnote. The KJV tradition reads "fifty thousand and seventy men" (50,070).
- **The manuscript evidence is thoroughly discussed on StudyLight.org**, which assembles the major witnesses:
  - **Josephus** mentions only **70** fatalities. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-samuel/6-19.html)
  - **Several Hebrew manuscripts** (from Holland, Paris, Milan, 12th century) omit "fifty thousand men." (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-samuel/6-19.html)
  - **The Vulgate** has "seventy men of the chief people, and fifty thousand of the common people." **The Targum** similarly distinguishes "elders" from "congregation." **The Syriac** reads 5,070. **The Arabic** reads 5,070. **The LXX** retains 50,070. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-samuel/6-19.html)
  - **Keil & Delitzsch** conclude the number 50,000 "is neither correct nor genuine, but a gloss which has crept into the text through some oversight." They argue: the 70 stands before the 50,000 (unusual), the copula *vav* is omitted (unparalleled), 50,000 people could not possibly live in or around Beth-shemesh, and the words are missing in key Hebrew MSS. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/1-samuel-6.html)
  - **One proposed solution**: supply the comparative particle *k* ("like, as"), yielding "seventy men, equal to fifty thousand men" — i.e., they were elders or governors whose loss was as weighty as 50,000. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-samuel/6-19.html)
  - **Another proposal** (Bochart, Waterland, Patrick): read "seventy men; fifty out of a thousand" — God smote only a twentieth part of the offenders. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-samuel/6-19.html)
  - **Constable** (Dallas Theological Seminary) notes the number may represent a scribal error; several modern translations state only 70. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-samuel-6.html — from search excerpt)
  - **Guzik**: "The manuscript evidence is pretty clear that the number recorded originally in the text was seventy, not fifty thousand and seventy. Seventy men dead in such an incident is still a great slaughter." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-6/)

---

### v. 20–21: "Who can stand in the presence of the LORD, this holy God?… Come down and take it up with you."

- **Guzik** notes the men of Beth-shemesh asked a **mixed question**. On one hand, "Who can stand before this holy LORD God?" is the right question — God is holy, and no sinner can stand before Him. On the other hand, they revealed a "bad heart" by blaming God's strictness rather than their own sin. Instead of asking "How can we be made right with a holy God?" they asked "Who can we give this problem to?" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-6/)
- **Trapp** (cited by Guzik): "Here they seem peevishly to lay the blame of their sufferings upon God, as over-holy and strict: of their sins, the true cause, they say nothing; but take care to rid their hands of the ark, which they should have retained reverently." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-6/)
- **Ellicott** sees something more positive: "Through their superstition we can discern a deep consciousness of sin and shortcoming, which argued well for the future reformation of the religious life of the people." He compares their fear to John falling as dead before the glorified Christ (Rev 1:17), but notes they "had no Redeemer there to raise them up with the loving whisper: 'Fear not.'" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/6.htm)
- **The Pulpit Commentary** adds: "Their request to the inhabitants of Kirjath-jearim… was the expression of something more than selfish dread, being caused by the belief that it would be more worthily honoured by others than by themselves." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/1_samuel/6.htm)
- **Keil & Delitzsch** note the subject of the verb "go up" (*ya'aleh*) is not the ark but **Jehovah Himself** — "to whom shall He go away from us?" The Beth-shemeshites recognized their unholiness before the holy God and sought to remove themselves from His presence. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/1-samuel-6.html)
- **Ligonier** (Reformed): "The Israelites came to a fresh appreciation of Yahweh's holiness because these men died… The last part of this verse indicates that they wished God would depart from them, because they were sinful and He was holy (cf. Isaiah 6:5)." (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/ark-returns-to-israel)
- **Kiriath-jearim** ("city of woods"): The ark remained there for about **seventy years** until David brought it to Jerusalem (2 Sam 6). It was placed in the house of Abinadab on the hill, under the guardianship of his consecrated son Eleazar. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/1_samuel/6.htm)

---

## Summary of Distinctive Interpretative Points by Tradition

### Reformed / Ligonier
- Emphasizes that the ark was **not a talisman**; God cannot be manipulated. Both Philistines and Israelites learned this. "The Bible reveals a God who cannot be manipulated by human beings." (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/ark-returns-to-israel)
- Sees the Beth-shemesh judgment as a result of treating the ark with contempt by those who should have known the law.

### Pentecostal / Charismatic (Enduring Word / David Guzik)
- Stresses the **miraculous** nature of the cows' journey as a sign that forces even pagans to acknowledge God's power.
- Reads the lowing cows as a devotional picture: "even in obedience, we can experience internal conflict, yet we serve a God with good purpose."
- Applies the Beth-shemeshites' fear of holiness to the New Testament: "Holiness is not so much something we have, it is something that has us… we are invited to be partakers — sharers of Jesus' holiness (Hebrews 12:10)."

### Lutheran / Keil & Delitzsch
- Takes a more cautious, text-critical approach. Argues that "looked at the ark" means irreverent staring, not opening it.
- Firmly rejects the 50,070 reading as a textual gloss.
- Sees the Philistine priests' test as an unwitting occasion for God to display His glory.

### Anglican / Ellicott
- Provides substantial historical and cultural context (ancient votive offerings, classical parallels).
- Reads "looked into" as opening the ark, possibly after drunken festivities.
- Has a pastoral, Christ-centered conclusion: the Beth-shemeshites lacked a Redeemer, unlike believers who have Christ's "Fear not."

### Broad Evangelical (Precept Austin / Bergen / Constable)
- Bergen emphasizes the **syncretism** of the Philistine priests — blending pagan magic with garbled Torah knowledge.
- Constable notes the possible connection to **bubonic plague** (fleas on rodents transmitting disease causing buboes/tumors), a theory many commentators mention. Josephus diagnosed the condition as dysentery. (from search excerpt, https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-samuel-6.html)
- The fertility motif: "Yahweh Himself appears as sovereign and all-powerful. Whereas the ark was the symbol of God's presence, it was not a talisman."

### On the Sacrifice at Beth-shemesh (v. 14): A Notable Disagreement
- **Guzik**: The sacrifice was technically against Mosaic law (female animals, away from tabernacle), but God "winked at" it given the extraordinary circumstances.
- **Ellicott, Keil & Delitzsch**: The sacrifice was **not a violation at all** — the presence of the ark of the covenant itself sanctified the location as the "throne of the gracious presence of God," making it as legitimate as offering at the tabernacle.
